source_quotes.quote: To gain a detailed insight into the reaction mechanism, we performed density functional theory (DFT) calculations using the ORCA 5.0.3 quantum chemical software package [46, 47]. All the calculations were carried out with the B3LYP [48–51] functional in combination with Grimme’s D3 dispersion correction and Becke–Johnson (BJ) damping [52, 53]. Solvent effects were incorporated implicitly using the SMD solvation model [54] with DCM as the solvent (For more details, see Supporting Information: Section 3). Furthermore, to understand electron transfer events, intrinsic bonding orbital (IBO) analysis was carried out using the IBOview software [55]. In addition, non-covalent interactions (NCI) analysis was carried out using the Multiwfn program [56], and the corresponding NCI isosurface plots were visualized with the VMD 1.9.3 program [57]. Our mechanistic investigation focused on the N–H insertion pathway of quinoxalin-2(1H)-one in the presence of a triplet carbene within aryl ester labelled as <sup>3</sup>Int.1 in Figure 2A. The reaction initiates with the H-atom abstraction via a transition state ^ 3 \mathrm { T S } _ { 1 2 } with ∆G of 11.4 kcal mol<sup>−1</sup> relative to <sup>3</sup>Int.1, leading to the formation of <sup>3</sup>Int.2. Transition state ^ 3 \mathrm { T S } _ { 1 2 } , demonstrates the abstraction of a hydrogen atom from the N−H group of quinoxalin-2(1H)-one by the carbene carbon atom of the aryl ester in its triplet spin state. Furthermore, the H-atom abstraction step was investigated involving a singlet carbene within the aryl ester in the presence of quinoxalin-2(1H)-one, denoted as <sup>1</sup>Int.1. (For more information, see Figure S5 in Supporting Information) This transformation proceeds via transition state ^ 1 \mathrm { T S } _ { 1 2 } with ∆G of 1.6 kcal mol<sup>−1</sup> relative to <sup>3</sup>Int.1. However, this leads to the formation of thermodynamically less favored intermediate, 1Int.2 with ∆G of −5.2 kcal \mathrm { m o l ^ { - 1 } } as compared \mathrm { \bf t o } ^ { 3 } \mathrm { I n t . } 2 . \mathrm { S o } , further reaction mechanism was subsequently explored along the triplet state. To obtain a deeper electronic understanding ofthe H-abstraction step, IBO analysis was carried out. The IBO analysis revealed that the hydrogen atom transfer proceeds via a radical pathway, indicating a homolytic cleavage of the N–H bond in quinoxalin-2(1H)-one as shown in Figure 2B. Further, quasi-restricted orbital (QRO) analysis was carried out to trace the positions of unpaired electrons in <sup>3</sup>Int.2. QRO analysis revealed that one electron is localized as a carbon-centered radical on the aryl ester, while the other electron is delocalized over the quinoxalin-2(1H)-one in intermediate <sup>3</sup>Int.2 (see Figure S6 in Supporting Information). In the subsequent O-alkylation step, the carbon-centered radical generated on the aryl ester combines with the carbonyl oxygen atom of quinoxalin-2(1H)-one via a transition state ^ 3 \mathrm { T S } _ { 2 3 } with a very high activation barrier of 33.7 kcal mol<sup>−1</sup> relative to <sup>3</sup>Int.2. This step leads to the formation of intermediate <sup>3</sup>Int.3, which lies at a relative Gibbs free energy of 12.1 kcal \mathrm { m o l ^ { - 1 } } . Further, QRO analysis revealed that one unpaired electron is delocalized over the benzene ring, while the other one is delocalized over the pyrazine ring of the quinoxalin-2(1H)-one. Subsequently, spin inversion of one of the unpaired electrons localized on the rings furnishes a closed-shell singlet intermediate, <sup>1</sup>Int.3, which resides significantly lower in energy, with a relative Gibbs energy of−47.3 kcal mol<sup>−</sup>1 (relative to 3Int.1).

Interestingly, we identified an alternative N-alkylation pathway proceeding via a lower-energy transition state ( ^ { 3 } \mathrm { T S } _ { 2 4 } ) , featuring an activation barrier of 25.8 kcal \mathrm { m o l ^ { - 1 } } , relative to <sup>3</sup>Int.2. This transition state ^ { 3 } \mathrm { T S } _ { 2 4 } , involves the coupling between N-centered radical of quinoxalin-2(1H)-one and carbon-centered radical on an aryl ester, resulting into the formation of <sup>3</sup>Int.4 with relative Gibbs energy of −5.1 kcal \mathrm { m o l ^ { - 1 } } (relative to <sup>3</sup>Int.1). Further, QRO analysis of <sup>3</sup>Int.4 showed a similar distribution of unpaired electrons as observed in the O-alkylation step. Further spin inversion in intermediate <sup>3</sup>Int.4, results in the formation of a closed-shell singlet intermediate, <sup>1</sup>Int.4, with a relative Gibbs energy of −58.5 kcal mol<sup>−</sup>1 (relative to 3Int.1).

Further, NCI analysis of the ^ 3 \mathrm { T S } _ { 2 3 } and ^ 3 \mathrm { T S } _ { 2 4 } transition states was conducted, corresponding to the O-alkylation and N-alkylation pathways, respectively (Figure 2C). This analysis reveals that the N-alkylation transition state is significantly stabilized via π−π stacking interactions, as indicated by the green isosurface between the phenyl rings of the aryl ester and quinoxalin-2(1H)-one. In contrast, the O-alkylation transition state exhibits comparatively weaker π−π interactions. These observations suggest that attractive Van der Waals interactions effectively stabilize the N-alkylation pathway. Thus, our computational studies provide detailed mechanistic insights into the N−H insertion of quinoxalin-2(1H)-one and highlight the role of attractive Van der Waals interactions in facilitating the N-alkylation pathway. These findings are consistent with experimental observation, as only the N-alkylated product was observed in experiments.

(B) FIGURE 2 (A) DFT-computed Gibbs energy profile for the N−H insertion of quinoxalin-2(1H)-one, computed at the SMD(DCM)-B3LYP-D3(BJ)/def2-TZVP//B3LYP-D3(BJ)/def2-SVP level of theory. All the numerical values in parenthesis are relative Gibbs energy (∆G) at 298.15 K, (B) intrinsic bonding orbital (IBO) analysis for the H-abstraction step along the intrinsic reaction coordinate, and (C) non-covalent interactions (NCI) analysis for the O-alkylation ( ^ { 3 } \mathrm { T S } _ { 2 3 } ) and N-alkylation ( ^ { 3 } \mathrm { T S } _ { 2 4 } ) transition states.

All computations were carried out using the ORCA 5.0.3<sup>[3,4]</sup> quantum chemical program package. Geometries were optimized with the hybrid-GGA functional with Becke threeparameter exchange<sup>[5]</sup> and Lee–Yang–Parr correlation<sup>[6]</sup> in conjunction with def2-SVP<sup>[7]</sup> basis sets. To accelerate the calculations, the resolution-of-the-identity approximation for the Coulomb term (RIJ) with a chain of sphere (COS) algorithm (RIJCOSX) is applied to the Hartree–Fock (HF) exchange (X) part of the approximation.<sup>[8]</sup> The atom-pairwise dispersion correction with Beck Johnson (D3BJ) was employed to include noncovalent interactions.<sup>[9]</sup> During the geometry optimization or frequency calculations, all the atoms were relaxed. Subsequent numerical frequency calculations were undertaken for the optimized geometries to confirm that they correspond to stationary points featuring no imaginary frequencies, whereas only one imaginary frequency confirmed the transition state structure. Gibbs energies were calculated by single point calculations with B3LYP-D3BJ/def2-TZVP<sup>[10]</sup> method on the B3LYP-D3BJ/def2-SVP geometries. The SMD continuum solvation model<sup>[11]</sup> was employed to account for the influence of the implicit solvent, dichloromethane, on the computed Gibbs free energy profiles. All reported numerical values correspond to relative Gibbs free energies obtained from mechanistic calculations carried out at the SMD(dichloromethane)-B3LYP-D3BJ/def2- TZVP//SMD(dichloromethane)-B3LYP-D3BJ/def2-SVP level of theory. To gain further insights into the electronic structure, quasi-restricted orbitals (QROs) were analyzed using the ORCA quantum chemistry program. In addition, non-covalent interaction (NCI) analysis were performed using the Multiwfn software<sup>[12]</sup>, and the corresponding NCI isosurfaces were visualized with VMD 1.9.3<sup>[13]</sup>.

Conclusion 
In summary, we have developed a visible-light-mediated, 
transition-metal-free protocol for the direct N–H alkylation 
of quinoxalin-2(1H)-ones using aryl diazo esters as alkylating 
agents. The reaction proceeds under mild conditions with broad 
substrate scope, good functional group tolerance, and without the 
need for external photocatalysts or additives. Mechanistic and 
computational studies support the involvement of a photoexcited 
triplet carbene intermediate, with π–π stacking interactions 
governing selectivity. This operationally simple and sustainable 
method offers a practical route to N-alkylated quinoxalinones, 
enabling late-stage functionalization of pharmaceutically 
relevant scaffolds.

computation_relevance: The authors' DFT study directly addresses the same reaction system and selectivity phenomenon: N-H functionalization of quinoxalin-2(1H)-one with an aryl diazo ester-derived carbene intermediate in DCM. They computed competing O-alkylation and N-alkylation pathways, reported relative Gibbs free energies for the relevant transition states and intermediates, and used NCI analysis to compare transition-state stabilization. These results can serve as private evaluation references for explaining the observed N-alkylation selectivity.

All computations were carried out using the ORCA 5.0.3<sup>[3,4]</sup> quantum chemical program package. Geometries were optimized with the hybrid-GGA functional with Becke threeparameter exchange<sup>[5]</sup> and Lee–Yang–Parr correlation<sup>[6]</sup> in conjunction with def2-SVP<sup>[7]</sup> basis sets. To accelerate the calculations, the resolution-of-the-identity approximation for the Coulomb term (RIJ) with a chain of sphere (COS) algorithm (RIJCOSX) is applied to the Hartree–Fock (HF) exchange (X) part of the approximation.<sup>[8]</sup> The atom-pairwise dispersion correction with Beck Johnson (D3BJ) was employed to include noncovalent interactions.<sup>[9]</sup> During the geometry optimization or frequency calculations, all the atoms were relaxed. Subsequent numerical frequency calculations were undertaken for the optimized geometries to confirm that they correspond to stationary points featuring no imaginary frequencies, whereas only one imaginary frequency confirmed the transition state structure. Gibbs energies were calculated by single point calculations with B3LYP-D3BJ/def2-TZVP<sup>[10]</sup> method on the B3LYP-D3BJ/def2-SVP geometries. The SMD continuum solvation model<sup>[11]</sup> was employed to account for the influence of the implicit solvent, dichloromethane, on the computed Gibbs free energy profiles. All reported numerical values correspond to relative Gibbs free energies obtained from mechanistic calculations carried out at the SMD(dichloromethane)-B3LYP-D3BJ/def2- TZVP//SMD(dichloromethane)-B3LYP-D3BJ/def2-SVP level of theory. To gain further insights into the electronic structure, quasi-restricted orbitals (QROs) were analyzed using the ORCA quantum chemistry program. In addition, non-covalent interaction (NCI) analysis were performed using the Multiwfn software<sup>[12]</sup>, and the corresponding NCI isosurfaces were visualized with VMD 1.9.3<sup>[13]</sup>.

Conclusion 
In summary, we have developed a visible-light-mediated, 
transition-metal-free protocol for the direct N–H alkylation 
of quinoxalin-2(1H)-ones using aryl diazo esters as alkylating 
agents. The reaction proceeds under mild conditions with broad 
substrate scope, good functional group tolerance, and without the 
need for external photocatalysts or additives. Mechanistic and 
computational studies support the involvement of a photoexcited 
triplet carbene intermediate, with π–π stacking interactions 
governing selectivity. This operationally simple and sustainable 
method offers a practical route to N-alkylated quinoxalinones, 
enabling late-stage functionalization of pharmaceutically 
relevant scaffolds.

source_quotes.quote: To evaluate the viability of the proposed N–H insertion reaction, we carried out a reaction between quinoxalin-2(1H)-one (1a, 0.1 mmol) and methyl 2-diazo-2-phenylacetate (2a, 2.5 equiv) as model substrates in chloroform at ambient temperature in the presence of 467 nm blue LED light (see Supporting Information: Table S1 for complete optimization studies, Figure S1 for a representative image of the reaction set up, and Figure S2 for UV-Vis studies on the reaction components). Pleasingly, the reaction completed in 3 h, providing the desired N-alkylated quinoxalinone 3aa in 35% isolated yield (Table 1, entry 1). Motivated by this initial result, we investigated the impact of solvent polarity on the reaction outcome. In particular, polar solvents, such as DMSO and methanol, fully inhibited product formation (entries 2 and 3), presumably due to either quenching of the reactive carbene intermediates or interfering with the diazo decomposition pathway. While trace product formation was observed in ethyl acetate, no further improvement was detected in acetonitrile, a frequently used solvent in photochemical reactions (entries 4–5). Encouragingly, the yield escalated to 40% in 1,2-dichloroethane (DCE), and dichloromethane (DCM) as the solvent provided 72% yield of 3aa (entries 6–7). While reducing the loading of the diazo compound had a detrimental effect on the outcome of the reaction, no product formation was observed when the reaction was carried out in the dark (entries 8–10). Notably, addition of commonly used organic and inorganic bases did not impart beneficial outcome, rather a substantial decrease in the yield of the product was observed (see Table S1 in the Supporting Information).

We report a visible-light-induced, metal-free approach to the selective N-alkylation of quinoxalin-2(1H)-ones using aryl diazo esters. This mild, catalyst-free protocol runs under ambient conditions and allows access to a wide variety of N-alkylated products with excellent functional group tolerance. Mechanistic studies suggest the formation of a donor–acceptor carbene intermediate that undergoes selective N–H insertion. This study illustrates the usefulness of visible-light activation of aryl diazo esters and their utilization as alkylating agents to achieve N–H bond functionalization in heterocycles in a sustainable and efficient manner. Density functional theory calculations provide insight into the mechanism and elucidate the role of π−π interactions in facilitating the reaction.

Pleasingly, the reaction completed in 3 h, providing the desired N-alkylated quinoxalinone 3aa in 35% isolated yield (Table 1, entry 1). Motivated by this initial result, we investigated the impact of solvent polarity on the reaction outcome. In particular, polar solvents, such as DMSO and methanol, fully inhibited product formation (entries 2 and 3), presumably due to either quenching of the reactive carbene intermediates or interfering with the diazo decomposition pathway. While trace product formation was observed in ethyl acetate, no further improvement was detected in acetonitrile, a frequently used solvent in photochemical reactions (entries 4–5). Further, NCI analysis of the ^ 3 \mathrm { T S } _ { 2 3 } and ^ 3 \mathrm { T S } _ { 2 4 } transition states was conducted, corresponding to the O-alkylation and N-alkylation pathways, respectively (Figure 2C). This analysis reveals that the N-alkylation transition state is significantly stabilized via π−π stacking interactions, as indicated by the green isosurface between the phenyl rings of the aryl ester and quinoxalin-2(1H)-one. In contrast, the O-alkylation transition state exhibits comparatively weaker π−π interactions. These observations suggest that attractive Van der Waals interactions effectively stabilize the N-alkylation pathway. Thus, our computational studies provide detailed mechanistic insights into the N−H insertion of quinoxalin-2(1H)-one and highlight the role of attractive Van der Waals interactions in facilitating the N-alkylation pathway. These findings are consistent with experimental observation, as only the N-alkylated product was observed in experiments.
